evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.37: quī moderātiōne et cōnstantiā quiētus animō est (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fam. 9.11.1: firmitās et cōnstantia (Lewis & Short, s.v. firmitās)
terms.comment: Firmness of character that holds to its course; it is also consistency and steadiness in general (see constant-steady, consistent).
Keeping on with what one has rightly decided; Cicero sets it against pertinācia, obstinacy in what one should give up (Inv. 2.165; see stubborn).

evidence: Cic. Prov. Cons. 41: quae ego omnia obstinātiōne sententiae repudiāvī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Firmness in a good or a bad sense; obstinātō animō (or obstinātā mente) is “with a set mind, determinedly”.

evidence: Enn. ap. Cic. Off. 1.38: eōrundem mē lībertātī parcere certum est (Lewis & Short, s.v. certus)
terms.comment: The spoken way to say “I’m determined to, I’ve made up my mind to”; Lewis & Short: mostly before Cicero, most frequent in Plautus.

phrases.latin: persevērantia est in ratiōne bene cōnsīderātā stabilis et perpetua permānsiō
phrases.english: perseverance is standing firm and lasting in a well-considered plan
but bear it with a set mind, hold out

phrases.latin: Certum est mihi hoc hodiē perficere.
phrases.english: I’m determined to finish this today.
